# [SYNTHETIC FIXTURE] Structured Reading Logs and Source Credibility Judgments in First-Year Composition

SYNTHETIC STUDY NOTICE: This document is a fictional example created for a literature-review workflow demonstration. The authors, data, and results do not exist. Do not cite as real research.

Authors: Mara Alvarez (synthetic), J. Kim (synthetic)
Year: 2023

## Abstract

This synthetic cluster-randomized trial assigned first-year composition sections to a structured reading log or to an unstructured reading journal. Students in the structured log condition completed prompts on authorship, purpose, evidence, and corroboration for each assigned source.

## Methods

Twelve course sections were randomized, six to each condition, with 284 students completing both pretest and posttest. Source evaluation was measured with a performance task in which students rated and justified the credibility of four web sources.

## Results

Students using the structured reading log scored higher on the posttest source evaluation task than students keeping unstructured journals, with a standardized mean difference of d = 0.42.

The largest gain appeared on the corroboration subscale, where structured log students were more likely to check claims against a second source.

## Limitations

Instructors were not blinded to condition, and the performance task was scored by raters who knew the study hypotheses.

# [SYNTHETIC FIXTURE] Do Reading Logs Transfer? Source Evaluation on an Unprompted Delayed Task

SYNTHETIC STUDY NOTICE: This document is a fictional example created for a literature-review workflow demonstration. The authors, data, and results do not exist. Do not cite as real research.

Authors: Elin Lindqvist (synthetic), P. Haddad (synthetic)
Year: 2024

## Abstract

This synthetic randomized experiment tested whether practice with a structured reading log improved source evaluation on a delayed task that did not provide the log prompts.

## Methods

A total of 156 undergraduates from introductory psychology were randomly assigned to complete three weekly structured reading logs or three weekly summaries. A delayed task administered five weeks later asked students to choose the most credible of several sources on a health topic without any prompts.

## Results

Structured log students outperformed summary students on an immediate prompted task, but on the delayed unprompted task the groups did not differ (d = 0.08).

Students in the log condition reported that the prompts felt like a worksheet to complete rather than a habit of reading.

## Limitations

The delayed task used a single health topic and may not reflect evaluation in students' own disciplines.

# [SYNTHETIC FIXTURE] Reading Logs in Higher Education: A Conceptual Overview

SYNTHETIC STUDY NOTICE: This document is a fictional example created for a literature-review workflow demonstration. The authors and arguments do not exist. Do not cite as real research.

Authors: Ana Moreau (synthetic)
Year: 2022

## Abstract

This synthetic conceptual essay describes structured reading logs as guided templates that ask students to record who produced a source, why it was produced, and what evidence supports its claims.

## Argument

Structured reading logs differ from open reading journals because they make the evaluative questions explicit and repeatable across readings.

The essay argues that logs are most useful when they are paired with discussion, since a template alone can become a compliance exercise.

# [SYNTHETIC FIXTURE] Reading Logs Versus Checklists for Evaluating Online Sources: A Quasi-Experimental Study

SYNTHETIC STUDY NOTICE: This document is a fictional example created for a literature-review workflow demonstration. The authors, data, and results do not exist. Do not cite as real research.

Authors: Chidi Okafor (synthetic), L. Brandt (synthetic)
Year: 2024

## Abstract

This synthetic quasi-experiment compared a structured reading log with a CRAAP-style evaluation checklist in two sections of an undergraduate research methods course.

## Methods

The structured log section enrolled 61 students and the checklist section enrolled 58 students. Outcomes were coded from annotated bibliographies submitted at the end of the term.

## Results

Students in the structured log section cited more peer-reviewed and primary sources in their annotated bibliographies, but the difference from the checklist section was small and not statistically significant (p = 0.18).

Coders judged that structured log annotations more often explained why a source was trustworthy rather than simply listing checklist criteria.

## Limitations

Sections were taught by different instructors and were not randomized, so instructor effects cannot be separated from the intervention.

# [SYNTHETIC FIXTURE] Feedback Matters: Instructor Comments on Structured Reading Logs and Lateral Reading

SYNTHETIC STUDY NOTICE: This document is a fictional example created for a literature-review workflow demonstration. The authors, data, and results do not exist. Do not cite as real research.

Authors: Hiro Tanaka (synthetic), S. Achterberg (synthetic)
Year: 2025

## Abstract

This synthetic three-arm randomized trial compared structured reading logs with instructor feedback, structured reading logs without feedback, and a no-log control in an undergraduate library instruction program.

## Methods

The trial randomized 210 students across three arms. The primary outcome was the proportion of students who left an unfamiliar website to investigate it elsewhere, a behavior known as lateral reading, during a recorded think-aloud task.

## Results

Lateral reading was observed in 46% of students in the log with feedback arm, 29% in the log without feedback arm, and 22% in the control arm.

The authors concluded that the benefit of the log depended on feedback that pointed students toward checking sources beyond the page itself.

## Limitations

Think-aloud protocols may have prompted more deliberate behavior than students would show during ordinary coursework.

# Protocol: Structured Reading Logs and Undergraduate Source Evaluation

> **SYNTHETIC EXAMPLE REVIEW.** Every study in this workspace is a fictional fixture created to demonstrate the literature-review workflow. No result here describes real research, and none of it should be cited.

## Research question

Do structured reading logs improve undergraduate students' source evaluation compared with unstructured reading journals, checklists, summaries, or no reading log?

## Inclusion criteria

- **Population:** undergraduate students in any discipline or course type.
- **Intervention:** a structured reading log, meaning a repeatable template with explicit evaluative prompts (authorship, purpose, evidence, corroboration) completed while reading assigned or self-selected sources.
- **Comparator:** unstructured journal, checklist, summary writing, or no log.
- **Outcome:** a measured source evaluation outcome (performance task, coded student writing, or observed evaluation behavior such as lateral reading).
- **Design:** randomized, cluster-randomized, or quasi-experimental studies with a comparison group. Conceptual pieces may be retained only as background context.
- **Language/date:** English; no date limit.

## Exclusion criteria

- Secondary school, graduate, or professional populations.
- Interventions without a structured, repeatable log template.
- Outcomes limited to self-reported confidence or satisfaction.
- No comparison condition (except background conceptual pieces).

## Criteria approval

Run in evaluation capture mode. The task instructions fixed the scope, so the scope checkpoint was not paused for interactive approval.

# Literature Review: Structured Reading Logs and Undergraduate Source Evaluation

> **SYNTHETIC EXAMPLE REVIEW.** All studies cited below are fictional fixtures written for a workflow demonstration. Their authors, samples, and results do not exist. Treat nothing here as evidence about real students.

**Research question**: Do structured reading logs improve undergraduate students' source evaluation compared with unstructured journals, checklists, summaries, or no log?

**Inclusion criteria**: Undergraduate students; a structured, repeatable reading log with explicit evaluative prompts; a comparison condition; a measured source evaluation outcome; English; no date limit.

**Searches executed**: No live database searches were run. The task called for synthetic example studies only, so the pool consists of six synthetic fixture records, documented in `protocol.md`.

## Thematic synthesis

### What counts as a structured reading log

Structured reading logs differ from open reading journals because they make the evaluative questions explicit and repeatable across readings (Moreau, 2022).

### Immediate effects on prompted tasks

Students using the structured reading log scored higher on the posttest source evaluation task than students keeping unstructured journals, with a standardized mean difference of d = 0.42 (Alvarez, 2023). The largest gain appeared on the corroboration subscale, where structured log students were more likely to check claims against a second source (Alvarez, 2023). An active checklist comparator narrowed the gap. Students in the structured log section cited more peer-reviewed and primary sources in their annotated bibliographies, but the difference from the checklist section was small and not statistically significant (p = 0.18) (Okafor, 2024). Coders judged that structured log annotations more often explained why a source was trustworthy rather than simply listing checklist criteria (Okafor, 2024).

### Transfer to unprompted evaluation

Durability is where the synthetic evidence is weakest. Structured log students outperformed summary students on an immediate prompted task, but on the delayed unprompted task the groups did not differ (d = 0.08) (Lindqvist, 2024). Students in the log condition reported that the prompts felt like a worksheet to complete rather than a habit of reading (Lindqvist, 2024).

### Feedback as a moderator

Lateral reading was observed in 46% of students in the log with feedback arm, 29% in the log without feedback arm, and 22% in the control arm (Tanaka, 2025). The authors concluded that the benefit of the log depended on feedback that pointed students toward checking sources beyond the page itself (Tanaka, 2025). A conceptual essay argues that logs are most useful when they are paired with discussion, since a template alone can become a compliance exercise (Moreau, 2022).

### Overall judgment

Within this synthetic set, structured logs look helpful on prompted, near-transfer tasks and weak or absent on delayed, unprompted ones. The comparator matters, and gains against a checklist are smaller than gains against an unstructured journal. Feedback appears to be the ingredient that turns a template into a reading habit. Every one of these conclusions is illustrative, because the underlying studies are fictional.

## Risk of bias and certainty

Each synthetic study carries a design weakness that limits confidence. One trial used unblinded instructors and hypothesis-aware raters, the quasi-experiment confounded instructor with condition, the transfer study used a single topic, and the feedback trial relied on think-aloud protocols that may inflate deliberate behavior. Certainty should be rated low even if these were real studies.

## Research gaps

- No synthetic study measured source evaluation in students' own disciplinary coursework over a full term, so ecological validity is untested.
- No study crossed feedback with comparator type, which leaves open whether feedback alone explains the checklist and journal differences.
- No study reported outcomes by prior information literacy instruction, so it is unknown who benefits most.

## Retrieval summary

All five included synthetic records have full-text fixtures in `papers/{id}/fulltext.md`, and none is abstract-only. No PDFs are missing. The one excluded record (a secondary school sample) needed no retrieval.
